gen_cost._doc: What a generation costs, so a sheet can be budgeted before it is fired. THREE MCP SERVERS AND TWO TIER LADDERS: gpt-image-2 (1k) and gpt-image-2-2k run the OLD model on the OLD ladder and nothing already generated against them changes meaning; gpt-image-25 (1k only) runs gpt-image-2.5. 2.5 KEPT EVERY PRICE AND MOVED THE LABELS - 2.5 'high' spends what gpt-image-2 'medium' spent and 2.5 'max' spends what gpt-image-2 'high' spent, so a tier name carried across servers means something else. Every texture in this file was generated at gpt-image-2 'medium' = 1,756 output tokens; on 2.5 that is 'high', which is why that is the 2.5 server's default. MEASURED HERE, not quoted: three separate 1024x1024 gpt-image-2 'medium' calls each returned output_tokens exactly 1756, and output tokens do not move with prompt length (input ran 757-1003 across the three).

gpt-image-2.5._note: Identical price at every tier. Flare is the fast default; Sunburst is 1.5-2x slower and claims tighter layout and edit control - the one to reach for on a pack sheet, where layout adherence is the whole game. Tokens at 1024x1024; the per-tier counts are third-party measurement (CellCog 2026-09-08) since OpenAI publishes only the $/1M rates and says its own calculator does not cover 2.5. The 'high' row is corroborated: gpt-image-2 'medium' measured 1756 here, and the re-grade puts 2.5 'high' at that same spend.

gpt-image-2._note: The old ladder, unchanged. Still the only 2k route. 'medium' is what everything in this file was generated at.

per_cell_usd_at_parity_tier._note: One 1024 generation split into a grid, at the 1,756-token tier ($0.0527). art_px_per_object is what the cell is actually WORTH - cell px x the median long-axis fill measured on a real drop. Divide THAT by the world size the thing is DRAWN at to get texels/unit, and that second step is what picks the grid: a 2.43-unit bench billboard needs 6x6 or better (facility/floor-tile is 73 texels/unit), while a 0.75-unit flat decal on emitted geometry is fine at 8x8 and gets 64 subjects for one generation. Verified on the PACKED sheets rather than the drops: median largest-blob share 1.0000 on both, no clip artefacts from --tol 4, borders_nonzero 0 - raw-drop misalignment never survives the packer, so do not reject a dense grid on how the drop looks.

style: STYLE — match style-flat.png: a flat-shaded stylized texture for a top-down moody-night roguelike. Matte flat colors, very dark and muted desaturated palette, low contrast, even flat ambient lighting, subtle fine film grain, simple clean shapes, minimal detail. ABSOLUTELY NO photorealism, no realistic or volumetric lighting, no glossy/specular reflections, no lens or camera effects, no soft photographic shadows or depth of field — it should look hand-painted and flat, like a 2D game tile.
style_prop: STYLE — match style-flat.png: a flat-shaded stylized object for a top-down moody-night roguelike. Matte flat colors, even flat ambient lighting, subtle fine film grain, simple clean shapes, minimal detail. The object's own manufactured colour must READ AS THAT COLOUR — keep it clearly saturated at a medium-dark value, do not grey it out, do not wash it toward the background. ABSOLUTELY NO photorealism, no realistic or volumetric lighting, no glossy/specular reflections, no lens or camera effects, no soft photographic shadows or depth of field — it should look hand-painted and flat, like a 2D game tile.
style_corp: CORP SUBJECT — contemporary premium corporate interior, circa now: clean rectilinear forms, large unbroken planes, fine consistent reveals and shadow gaps, no ornament. The materials of this world are floor-to-ceiling glazing, dark anodised aluminium, brushed stainless, matte white lacquer, pale oak veneer, polished concrete, low-pile charcoal carpet tile with a visible modular grid, and acoustic felt. Everything is new, maintained and expensive — no rust, no chipping, no grime, no clutter of age, no decay. Where an accent colour appears it is WARM — amber, brass, tan — and never blue, because the scene light is already blue and a near-neutral albedo wears the lamp's hue.
_style_doc: TWO strings, and which one you append depends on what the image IS. `style` is for a SURFACE — a tiling texture, a decal, a sprite sheet: a wall really is grey, so its 'very dark and muted desaturated palette, low contrast' clause is correct there and every one of the 203 shipped textures wears it. `style_prop` is for an OBJECT — a TRELLIS reference image, i.e. anything that becomes a glb: it is the same string with that one clause replaced by the opposite instruction, because an object's colour is a fact about the object and a manufactured thing that comes back grey is simply wrong. Measured before the split: 9 of 38 props carried a per-channel `baseColor` and every one of them shipped neutral, `wild/tree-broadleaf-full` losing a 41.5-chroma green canopy to 3.8 and `facility/trash-bin` a bottle-green body to 0.1. Append ONE of them verbatim to EVERY gpt-image-2 gen/edit prompt; keep both in sync with the texture-art-style memory, and keep every clause but the palette one identical between them. style_corp is a SUBJECT clause and NOT a third style: it is appended IN FRONT OF style (a corp surface) or style_prop (a corp object), never instead of one. It exists so a corp batch cannot drift between phases.
_doc: Source-of-truth for textures. src lives in textures-src/ (1024), output goes to textures/<label>.png. class: tile|window|chroma|sprite. needs_alpha -> tool warns if output is opaque. chroma -> key color baked to alpha before downscale. prompt_exact:false means the prompt was reconstructed, not the original. Run `make tex` after editing a source or this file.

city/sewer-hatch.note: the cast-iron lid on the pavement that leads down to the tunnels (objects.SewerHatch, entities64 row 2 col 0). IT IS A TEXTURE AND NOT A PROP, which is the silhouette-vs-surface test drawn through the flattest object in the game: AreaObject.isGroundDecal is true for a hatch, so the 3D street lays its sprite FLAT on the cell and there is no outline to buy - what carries it is the tread pattern, which is a surface. THE 1024 DROP IS CUT TO A HARD CIRCLE before it is adopted: gpt returned the cover out to the frame edges with a soft brown haze in the corners (alpha mean 192 over the whole square), so the source is masked to a disc and then inset to 94% of the cell, which is what makes it read as a lid lying on asphalt rather than one clipped by its own tile. The cell it replaces was near-black at 64 px; this measures rgb 68/61/53 over its own opaque 67% of the frame. DRAWN AT 256 AND NOT 64, through the third arm of render.particles.Sprites.atlasFor beside the bench and clue packs: a hatch spans Sprites.SIZE 3.0 world units, so a 64 px cell is 21 texels per world unit against city/ground-asphalt's own 57 - the blurriness art/textures.json's facility/floor-grate note records at 21.3, on the same number. At 256 it is 85. LIFT 0.75, and it is the one number here that was fitted LIVE rather than off the drop: a ground decal's crop is darkened by RenderConfig.DECAL.actorMul 0.7 before it is drawn, which is 0.45 in light, so the mid-dark lid the gen returned rendered at luma 8 against the pavement's 30 - 0.27x, i.e. the hole-in-the-ground failure this file's own `lift` header describes. The gamma takes built_linear 0.0505 to ~0.09 so the drawn lid lands about 0.6x the walkway it lies in: darker than the pavement, which a cast-iron lid is, and not a void. It is ONE CELL and not a pack, so there is no index table and no arithmetic: the image IS the cell, which is the whole difference between this and Const.FACILITY_DECO_HD. The 2D area view keeps drawing the entities64 frame, which tools/atlaspaste.py rewrites from the same source, so the two views stay the same object

wild/grass.note: the grass tufts (render.wild.WildGrass), on two crossed alpha-tested quads per tuft. SIDE-ON and rooted in the BOTTOM EDGE, which is the whole spec: the quad's v runs 0 at the ground to 1 at the tip, so blades that stopped short of the edge would float and a top-down lawn tile (the placeholder this replaces) reads as a flat patch pasted on the ground instead of standing grass. non-square res keeps the source's 4:3, matching TUFT_W 1.5 x TUFT_H 1.1. lift 1.4 is used BACKWARDS here and deliberately: the gamma is a plain power, so g > 1 DARKENS where every other entry uses g < 1 to lift. as painted the blades measure LINEAR luminance 0.1357 against the ground's lifted 0.0503 - 2.70x, which made the grass the brightest thing in the area apart from the actor, and well over the prop family's 46-52 sRGB. 1.4 lands them at 0.0660 (1.31x the ground, sRGB 73/71/53): still the lighter of the two, because out here nothing else supplies a value break, but in the same world as everything around it. NOTE the tuft quads carry straight-up normals (render.wild.WildGrass.tuft), so a blade takes exactly the GROUND's irradiance - the ratio above is a pure albedo ratio and this knob is the only thing that sets it. class SPRITE and NOT chroma, with the alpha hand-cut into the source: this subject cannot be keyed at all, because the blades' own mean colour (105/104/84) is INSIDE the key's tolerance of the background (max channel diff 15 against tol 24), so the key ate the grass along with the grey behind it.

facility/sink.note: the laboratory sinks on the bench runs (render.facility.FacilitySink) - a flat BASIN decal lying on the worktop and an upright FAUCET quad standing at its back edge, two quads on one bench cell. TWO CELLS ON ONE SHEET AND NOT TWO TEXTURES, for facility/exit-sign's and facility/placards' reason: two images are two materials, two meshes and two draw calls to draw one fixture, where a u/v sub-rect is four numbers. Measured in game: the whole family costs +1 draw call, 9 of 9 A/B pairs, and +0 programs - a mapped alpha-cut lambert is the permutation FacilityDeco.cut's shelving frame already warms. It is also the case the packed-sheet trap does NOT cover: docs/3d-textures.md warns a sheet cannot serve an alpha cut because background:transparent cuts the WHOLE image, and here BOTH cells want the cut, so the objection inverts into the argument for packing. NO SEAM TO MEASURE: the background is genuinely empty (69.80 percent of pixels at alpha 0, max alpha 254 - the API's own 253-not-255 ceiling), so each object's own ALPHA BBOX is its cell, padded outward 2px so the 1-2px edge ramp falls inside the rect and alphaTest 0.5 trims it rather than clipping the silhouette. Basin x 31..648 y 288..736 = 618x449, h/w 0.726537; tap x 670..1013 y 243..735 = 344x493, w/h 0.697769 - and THOSE are the aspects FacilityStyle.SINK_BASIN_D and SINK_FAUCET_W are locked to. The tap's column is not centred in its rect, the handle sticking out left and the spout arching right: its foot spans x 739..909, centre 824 against a rect centre of 841.5, so SINK_FAUCET_AXIS 0.05087 slides the quad and the tap STANDS on the cell centre instead of being hung by its bounding box. THE TAP IS THE SECOND ROLL AND THE FIRST ONE SHIPPED AS WIRE, which is this entry's real lesson. Drawn at honest proportions it came back 18.4 percent opaque over its rect at srgb 105.6, and in game it was a faint scribble on black resin - docs/3d-geometry.md's 'honest member width reads as WIRE', the shelving frame's own failure at 26 percent. Re-rolled SOLO at 640x1024 asking for massively thick members and naming srgb 160 outright, then PIL-pasted into the sheet with the basin left untouched: the placards' route and for their reason, an edit_image over the sheet redraws the cell that was already right. Second roll: opaque fraction 0.3290, srgb 156.4, channel spread 0.6 - perfectly neutral, against the basin's 4.4. NO lift on the label, because lift is per LABEL and the two cells want opposite moves; if the tap ever needs moving alone it is a per-cell gamma at composite time, the way facility/placards' prohibition disc was fixed. BUILT at the game camera against a bare worktop at srgb 32.9: basin FOOTPRINT (rim plus its shaded well, unthresholded) 56.7 = 1.72x, the rim alone 95.3, tap metal 116.1 = 3.53x. The tap reading well over the basin is correct and not a miss - it is polished steel standing up into the room light while the bowl is a shaded recess lying flat - and it lands in the same value family as the flask and scale sprites sharing its bench. RES 256 AND NOT 512, which is a DENSITY decision and not a memory one: the basin draws SINK_BASIN_W 2.5 world units from a 154-texel crop = 61.6 texels per world unit, and the bench sprites beside it sit at 59 (the number DECO_TABLE_SCALE was fitted to), so the sink now samples at the density of the family it shares a worktop with. The tap lands at 76.1. Halving the sheet moved neither value - footprint 55.7 -> 56.7 and tap 114.4 -> 116.1 on identically thresholded patches - because a box downscale averages texels and does not shift their mean. One cost, and it is why the 2px pad is quoted at the SOURCE and not the output: 2px at 1024 is half a texel at 256, so the silhouette now reaches the outermost texel row of both rects and alphaTest trims about one texel off each outer edge. At 61.6 texels per world unit that is 0.016 world units and invisible; a res below 256 would start eating the rim. BOTH CELLS WERE LATER RE-GAMMA'D, AND THE 'NO lift' LINE ABOVE IS EXACTLY WHY - reported from the game as the faucet being too bright, and it measured as the brightest thing on the worktop by a wide margin: at the game camera, p90 over its own patch 132.7 against the bench sprites sharing the bench at 61.7-64.0 and the capped worktop clutter at 68.0, i.e. ~1.45x the family this note claims it lands in. That claim was fitted before the bench packs were repainted and re-exposed, and it does not survive them. `lift` still cannot answer it (per LABEL, and the two cells want DIFFERENT moves, not opposite ones), so both took a per-cell gamma at composite time through the new tools/cellgamma.py - the placards route, promoted to a tool because this is the second sheet to need it. TAP gamma 2.0, source metal srgb 157.0 -> 98.8, on screen 93.7 -> 72.7. THEN THE BASIN RIM WAS THE BRIGHTEST THING LEFT, which the tap had been hiding: unchanged at 94.0 while the tap came down past it, so it took gamma 1.27, source srgb 84.7 -> 63.1, on screen 94.0 -> 66.0. Final family: tap 71.7, rim 66.0, against scale 64.0 and rack 61.7 UNCHANGED in the same frame - and those two controls not moving is what proves only the two rects moved. THE PRISTINE PRE-GAMMA SOURCE IS PARKED AT textures-src/facility/Unused/sink.png and every retune must start there: a gamma STACKS, so a second pass over the shipped source is a compound and not a correction. Rebuild with: python3 tools/cellgamma.py textures-src/facility/Unused/sink.png textures-src/facility/sink.png 670,1013,243,735=2.0 31,648,288,736=1.27

facility/wall-points.note: the two corridor wall fittings a keep-clear zone belongs to (render.facility.FacilityPoint): the fire point and the electrical panel. Same 0..1-cell discipline as facility/notice-board and facility/exit-sign - the fitting's own frame IS the cell border, and any margin gpt left round it would draw as wall-coloured nothing standing proud of the wall (measured: edge column/row means 31.2 / 33.1 / 31.4 / 29.9, so all four borders are frame). AN ATLAS AND NOT TWO TEXTURES, for exit-sign's own reason: two images are two materials, two meshes and two draw calls to change a pictogram, where a u sub-rect is four numbers. Cells are LEFT fire point (u 0..0.5) and RIGHT panel (u 0.5..1) - see POINT_U. The split is SIDE BY SIDE and not stacked because both fittings are PORTRAIT: each cell is 512x1024 in the source and the quad is POINT_W 2.0 by POINT_H 4.0, so the 1:2 aspect is the art's and nothing is stretched - and because the aspect is locked, that scale is the ONLY lever the family has on how big it reads, which is why it went 1.6 -> 2.0 on a report of the fittings not being seen at all. The model drew the divider at 509-514 rather than dead on 512 (largest column jump 54.6 at 514, against 26.9 for the next feature), so each half keeps about three dark columns of the other's frame on its inner edge - which reads as the fitting's own frame and is why no crop is needed. THE SOURCE IS HAND-EDITED AND THE LIFT IS DELIBERATELY NOT BAKED INTO IT. As generated the fire cell measured 107.6/32.0/28.1 for a chroma spread of 79.6; the drop in textures-src was then DESATURATED by hand to 93.4/45.1/42.5, spread 50.9, at IDENTICAL luma (0.0518 against 0.0519, which is why the change was invisible in the game - it moved chroma and not value). Because that file is edited by hand, the value knob stays HERE as a `lift` rather than as a gamma written into the source: baked in, it is lost on the next hand edit or applied twice. Ditto the reason it is one lift and not two - the bake has one per entry and the two cells are one entry, which is the price of the atlas that makes this family one draw call. lift 0.85 BRIGHTENS (g < 1) and the two halves land on values the compound already ships, against facility/wall-interior 0.1578, the corridor wall these hang on: the fire point 0.0518 -> 0.0729 = 0.33x -> 0.46x, exactly facility/notice-board's ratio, and the panel 0.0750 -> 0.0951 = 0.48x -> 0.60x, exactly facility/deco-cabinet-front's. A FITTING READS BELOW ITS OWN WALL here and both still do. THE PANEL IS WHAT CAPS THE LIFT and not the fire point: measured over the sweep, g 0.90 puts the panel at 0.60x and the fire point at only 0.41x, g 0.80 puts the fire point at 0.52x but the panel at 0.77x, and by g 0.70 the panel is 0.98x - the same value as the wall it hangs on. So the fire point can only be chased so far before the half that was already right stops being a fitting. sd 21.2 left and 15.3 right, both in facility/notice-board's placed-contrast band (34.3) rather than in a tiling surface's (wall-interior 3.0). A RE-ROLL of the left cell was proposed before the lift and was WRONG, off one frame where the fire point measured 0.0078 linear, 0.12x its wall - a stretch of corridor with no ceiling spot on it, generalised to the family. In a normally lit one the same fitting reads 0.0142 against a wall at 0.0550 = 0.26x at chroma 46.5. An indoor wall's value is a POSE number and not a surface one: measure a wall fitting in at least two poses before fitting anything to it, and note that a lift is still the right instrument once it IS wanted, because it moves the source ladder rather than chasing one pose's lighting.

facility/coping.note: the parapet's coping cap (render.facility.FacilityGeom.band). It wore facility/booth-roof for one build, which was the wrong material twice over: a kiosk's painted steel decking is a LID art stood on end, and it was picked for its VALUE rather than for what a coping is. Same VERTICAL-JOINTS, UNIFORM-TOP-TO-BOTTOM construction as facility/barrier-arm and the cabinet, and for the same reason - the coping is a box emitted through FacilityGeom.face and .cap on ONE period, so v is a thin horizontal slice of the image at an arbitrary offset (the 0.25-tall fascias sample y/9.0, i.e. 2.8% of the image) and a different one on the top cap (z/9.0). Uniform art makes every slice identical, so the joints line up across the cap and both fascias for free. THE DROP DID NOT TILE and was corrected in the source rather than re-rolled: gpt drew six stones on a 204.75 px pitch but cut the sixth joint at the frame edge, so the wrap put a half joint against a stone face - measured, left column against right column was 48.5/255. Cropped to four whole stones between two joint CENTRES and resampled back to 1024, both seams measure 0.00 - and then ROLLED half a stone, which is the second half of the same lesson: a joint sitting exactly ON the edge is split across the two sides, and the 1024 -> 512 downscale blends each half with its own neighbours only, so half a joint came back at each edge and the BUILT tile measured 7.88 against a 3.04 column step. Rolled 128 px the wrap lands on flat stone and the built tile measures 2.05, under its own noise. MEASURE THE BUILT FILE, not the source. At COPING_TILE 9.0 that is a 2.25-unit stone, 1.125 m at the half-metre unit. lift 1.83 DARKENS: as painted it is 0.2511 linear, the brightest source in the facility set and a white band at night, and 1.83 lands it on 0.0851 - the level the booth roof held after its own lift, 2.6x facility/wall-exterior, so the cap reads as a capping band rather than as an outline drawn round every building.

facility/barrier-arm.note: the boom barrier's hazard bands (render.facility.FacilityEntry), and the art that replaced a generated prop's atlas. VERTICAL BANDS, UNIFORM TOP TO BOTTOM, is the load-bearing part of the prompt and not a stylistic choice: the arm is a box emitted through FacilityGeom.face and .cap, which take ONE period for both axes, so on the sides v runs y/TILE over a 0.3-unit bar and on the top v runs z/TILE over a 0.34-unit one - both are thin horizontal SLICES of this image at arbitrary offsets. Uniform art makes every slice identical, so the bands line up across the top and the two sides for free and no second period is needed (contrast FacilityTables.panel, which needed one). Measured on the drop: max row deviation 0.010 against a mean of 0.311, i.e. 3.3%. It also tiles: the left edge is mid-red and the right edge white, so the wrap IS a band boundary. NOT LIFTED, and that is the interesting number. As painted the red bands are 0.0807 linear and the white 0.5453, a 6.8x ratio - which is exactly what the generated prop could not hold (its bake came back orange-on-tan and low-contrast, and baseColor is a per-channel multiply that cannot add contrast back). lift is a GAMMA and moves the two the wrong way round here: it darkens the ALREADY-DARK red far harder than the white, so lift 1.6 takes the red to 0.0276 - under the asphalt it stands over - and blows the ratio to 13.8x, which reads as white dashes floating with the red gone. The level is carried on the material's own color instead, which is a LINEAR multiply and holds the ratio - see BARRIER_TINT in FacilityStyle for the fitted number.

facility/barrier-post.prompt: A seamless tiling texture: the painted steel skin of a modern roadside equipment cabinet - the control housing at a vehicle barrier. CRITICAL: the slots RUN OFF THE TOP AND BOTTOM EDGES of the image and are cut off flat by them. They have NO rounded ends, NO closed ends, NO terminations, NO end caps, NO gaps anywhere - each slot is an unbroken straight channel from the very top edge of the image to the very bottom edge. The image must TILE SEAMLESSLY ON BOTH AXES, top to bottom as well as left to right: the top edge must join the bottom edge invisibly. Every horizontal slice of the image is identical to every other. There is no door outline, no hinge, no handle, no lock, no lid, no plinth, no bolts, no horizontal seam, no border, and no top-to-bottom shading gradient of any kind. Slightly weathered, with faint grime settled in the slots and a few small paint scuffs. Clearly darker and greener than pale grey roof decking. [append textures.json style]
facility/barrier-post.note: the boom barrier's control cabinet (render.facility.FacilityEntry). It wore facility/booth-roof for one build - the booth's own painted decking, on the argument that a machine housing standing beside a kiosk wants the kiosk's material - and that came straight back from the game as wanting art of its own, correctly: a LID material reads as a lid material stood on end. Same VERTICAL-SLOTS, UNIFORM-TOP-TO-BOTTOM construction as facility/barrier-arm and for exactly the same reason - the cabinet is a box emitted through FacilityGeom.face and .cap on ONE period, so v is a thin horizontal slice at an arbitrary offset on the sides (y/TILE) and a DIFFERENT one on the lid (z/TILE), and uniform art lines the louvres up all round for free. THE FIRST DROP IS WHY THE PROMPT NOW SPENDS A PARAGRAPH ON IT. Asked only for 'uniform from top to bottom' it drew the slots with ROUNDED ENDS a few pixels inside the top and bottom edges - which is a horizontal feature, and therefore a tile SEAM. It landed as a plain band with slot stubs under it 10% up the cabinet's faces, and crossed the LID somewhere else entirely, because v maps y on one and z on the other. A UV offset could only ever have hidden one of the two, and both move with the gate's world position, so a per-compound shift was not a fix: the ART was. Re-prompted with the slots stated to run OFF the edges and cut flat, and the tiling stated on BOTH axes: max row deviation 0.00150 linear against the first drop's 0.00706, a 4.7x improvement that puts it level with the arm, and the top and bottom rows now differ by 0.0078 per pixel, i.e. it really does tile vertically. NOT LIFTED: 0.0441 linear, between the asphalt it stands on (0.0329) and the park lawn (0.0414) and half the booth roof it used to wear (0.0849), so it reads as a dark green-grey box under a pale cap instead of as more of the cap. 16 slots over BARRIER_CAB_TILE 4.8 is a 0.3-unit pitch (15 cm at the half-metre unit) and 4 across a 1.2-unit face - deliberately coarse, because from 18-55 units up a realistic 7.5 cm louvre is one pixel and reads as noise. That constant is DERIVED FROM THE SLOT COUNT: a repaint dealing a different one has to move it or the pitch changes underneath.

facility/floor-lino.note: corridors and every door cell (Const.TILE_FLOOR_LINO). THE VALUE IS UNTOUCHED AND THAT IS THE POINT: lift 1.38 takes the new drop's 0.2358 linear to 0.1365, the same target the grey roll was fitted to, which is DERIVED and not chosen - the room's own floor:wall ratio (0.12 / 0.1394 = 0.861) applied to the corridor's own wall, facility/wall-interior at 0.1595. So the corridor still reads as light walls over a slightly darker floor exactly as a room does and still sits at 1.14x the room tile; only the hue moved. Drop 116.9/135.5/140.3, and 86.9/106.6/111.8 after the gamma. THE 24.9 BYTE SPREAD IS DELIBERATE AND DOES NOT BREAK THE >6 RE-ROLL RULE: that rule is about a cast nobody asked for, which a lift then publishes - here the cast IS the brief, so the gamma widening it from 23.4 is the knob working and not the failure it was on the olive drop. The 'ask for a value, not a word' spec still applies and is why the prompt names the bytes outright (88/104/112) rather than saying 'light blue'. Measured in one corridor frame against its own wall in the same lighting band: floor 60.2/95.5/107.2 (G-B -11.7) against facility/wall-interior at 66.4/77.2/79.9 (G-B -2.7, the number every neutral surface here sits at because the rig is blue). Value it can: measured, the drop's gap came back 0.1575 linear against the corridor lino's 0.1353, which is 1.16x and close. HUE it cannot - facility/floor-lino is deliberately a pale blue-cyan (roughly r88 g104 b112) and a neutral grey band on it reads as a different material however well the value lands. WITH A CUT THE `color` TINT BECOMES POSSIBLE AGAIN and is deliberately not taken here: a tint only multiplies what survives alphaTest, so neutral stripes plus one uniform per mesh would serve red and yellow off one map. Tiling is approximate and deliberately accepted: the drop came back nearer 34 degrees than 45 (6 stripe transitions across the top edge against 4 down the left, where a true 45 gives the same count both ways), so the two axes cannot both close on a whole period - measured wrap error 3.1/255 on x and 7.2 on y, which does not show because a zone is 4x3 world units against a ZONE_TILE 3.0 repeat and shows about one repeat.

facility/deco-shelf-side.prompt: The END FRAME of a HEAVY-DUTY industrial steel shelving unit, seen straight on from the side, flat elevation. The uprights and the rails reach right to the left and right borders of the image. Everything between the rails is open air with nothing in it. Dark cool grey galvanised steel, matte, faint scuffs and a few bolt heads. No shelves, no boxes, no floor, no wall, no shadow. [append textures.json style]
facility/deco-shelf-side.note: the shelving's two end frames (render.facility.FacilityDeco). ALPHA, and the one cut surface in the family: the frame is what a steel unit's side actually is, and the holes are what let the room show through it - which is also why there is no back panel. Mapped 0..1 over the end face rather than tiled, because it is ONE authored frame; that locks DECO_SHELF_D to the source's 656 x 1024 aspect. 656 wide is also the narrowest gpt-image-2 will emit at 1k - a source must clear 655,360 px with no edge over 1024, which caps the aspect near 0.64. Generated with background:transparent; measured 76.2% of pixels under alpha 128. lift 0.771 BRIGHTENS (a gamma, g < 1): at its painted 61 opaque-mean the frame's own members rendered as near-black threads on a vertical face and the unit read as a wire cage rather than as steel angle - the art is chunky slotted uprights and 4 rails, and none of that survived the ~0.2 albedo-to-screen ratio an interior vertical face has here. REGENERATED with heavy members: at ~4.6% upright width the frame drew 0.077 world units of steel per upright, which is honest angle iron and read on screen as a WIRE CAGE. 12% uprights and 5% rails take the opaque fraction 26% -> 39%. Rails re-measured after the roll and DECO_SHELF_Y follows them, not the other way round.

facility/deco-shelf-top.prompt: A SEAMLESS TILEABLE texture of a perforated steel shelf panel seen from DIRECTLY ABOVE, flat top-down, no perspective. The pattern must tile seamlessly on both axes with no visible border and no frame. No edges, no lip, no brackets, no objects standing on it. [append textures.json style]
facility/deco-shelf-top.note: the shelving's shelves. It ALSO carried the server rack's sides and top - same perforated steel, same buffer, same draw call - until the rack read as a server made out of shelves and took its own facility/deco-rack-side and facility/deco-rack-top. TOP-DOWN art on purpose: it is laid flat far more often than not, and the first build put a side-elevation sheet here. No lip in the art, because a shelf is emitted as a bare quad with no thickness. DECO_SHELF_TILE 0.55 is a perforation pitch and nothing to do with the unit's own size. NOW CUT FROM facility/deco-pack4.png, the 2x2 sheet this tile shares with deco-box, deco-bookcase-side and deco-bookcase-top (crop 512,0,512,512). Four 512 tiles out of ONE 1024 generation - a quarter of the cost, and exactly the resolution the runtime ships at; measured on screen against the four solo sources the bookcase differed by mean |d| 0.5 / 255. Two prices: tiling wrap error roughly doubles, because a quadrant was composed to butt against its NEIGHBOURS and not against itself (3.4-4.5 H / 3.8-9.9 V against the solo rolls' 1.2-2.5 / 2.0-4.3), and a quadrant is square, so an aspect-locked 0..1 face or an alpha cut still takes its own image. lift 0.846 lands it at built mean 73.4, the value the solo roll shipped at, so the swap changed the ART and not the exposure.

No text, no letters, no numbers, no printed labels, no logos, no fragile symbols, no box edges or corners. [append textures.json style]
facility/deco-box.note: the boxes on the shelving's shelves. Its OWN texture and not the shelving's steel, which is what the first build did and what made a shelf of cardboard cartons read as more of the unit. Tiled at WORLD scale along each turned box face (DECO_BOX_TILE 0.5) rather than mapped 0..1 across it, so the yaw jitter never stretches it and no two boxes show the same patch. NOW CUT FROM facility/deco-pack4.png, the 2x2 sheet this tile shares with deco-shelf-top, deco-bookcase-side and deco-bookcase-top (crop 0,0,512,512). Four 512 tiles out of ONE 1024 generation - a quarter of the cost, and exactly the resolution the runtime ships at; measured on screen against the four solo sources the bookcase differed by mean |d| 0.5 / 255. Two prices: tiling wrap error roughly doubles, because a quadrant was composed to butt against its NEIGHBOURS and not against itself (3.4-4.5 H / 3.8-9.9 V against the solo rolls' 1.2-2.5 / 2.0-4.3), and a quadrant is square, so an aspect-locked 0..1 face or an alpha cut still takes its own image. lift 0.956 lands it at built mean 87.5, the value the solo roll shipped at, so the swap changed the ART and not the exposure. AND THE PACK IS WHAT FIXED THE CHROMA. A chroma target is unreachable from prose and three solo rolls prove it: 'warm tan-brown' returned R-B 67 at mean 108, 'greyed dusty, very low chroma' returned R-B 8.5 at 66.5, and naming the number outright ('the red channel about 25 to 30 points above the blue') returned R-B 58.6 at 112. `lift` cannot split the difference either - it is a GAMMA, so it scales a cast rather than shrinking it (at g 1.28 the warm roll's R-B goes 58.6 -> 59.3) - so what shipped for months was the NEUTRAL roll separated from the steel by VALUE alone. Drawn BESIDE the grey steel in one frame the model differentiated the two by itself: channel spread 48, and the boxes finally read as cardboard.

facility/deco-bookcase-front.prompt:

Hard butt joins on those two lines. NO gutters, NO margins, NO borders, NO frames, NO drop shadows, NO separator lines, NO labels, NO text, NO numbers. All three regions are the same dark warm grey-brown wood and must read as parts of ONE piece of furniture, but the BOOKS must be clearly separated from the WOOD in both colour and value - the carcass is dull matte timber, the spines carry what little colour there is.

LEFT REGION (the wide left three quarters, full height) - the complete front of the bookcase, seen straight on, flat elevation, FILLING THAT REGION EDGE TO EDGE with no margin and no wall visible around it. THREE horizontal shelves stacked one above another, each holding a tightly packed row of upright book spines, and the three rows must be CLEARLY DIFFERENT from one another: different mixes of spine width, height and colour, one row with a few volumes leaning into a small gap, one row with two books lying flat across the top of the upright ones. The books are SMALL relative to the region - each row of books is only about a quarter of the region's height. Muted desaturated book colours: dull ochre, faded maroon, olive, slate blue, greyed cream. Each spine carries only a faint illegible band or line suggesting a title - NEVER readable words, NEVER letters, NEVER numbers. Dark warm-grey wood shelf boards between the rows, one board across the very top edge and one across the very bottom edge, and a narrow wooden upright at the far left and far right edges of this region.

TOP-RIGHT REGION (upper half of the narrow right quarter) - a SEAMLESS TILEABLE swatch of the bookcase's side panel, seen straight on, flat elevation. Plain veneered board with a fine VERTICAL wood grain, a few faint scratches, a dull matte finish. NO books, no shelves, no hardware, no joints, no edges.

BOTTOM-RIGHT REGION (lower half of the narrow right quarter) - a SEAMLESS TILEABLE swatch of the bookcase's top board seen from DIRECTLY ABOVE, flat top-down, no perspective. Plain veneered wood boards with a fine grain, a light film of dust, a couple of faint ring marks and a few small scuffs. NO books, no objects, no edges, no shelf below. [append textures.json style]
facility/deco-bookcase-front.note: the bookcase's front, mapped 0..1 over the face - ONE authored composition with three DIFFERENT rows in it, which is the whole reason it is not tiled. The first build tiled a single bay at half the unit's height and got two identical rows of books at twice the size. That LOCKS DECO_BOOKCASE_W to the crop's 616 x 1024, and it is why `fit` slides a unit along its wall rather than clamping its width: a clamp would squeeze this image. CUT FROM facility/deco-bookcase-pack.png, one 1024 generation carrying the bookcase's WHOLE family: the front on the left, the side panel top-right, the top board bottom-right. Drawn together on purpose - the same trick that finally separated the shelving's cardboard from its steel separates these BOOKS from their CARCASS, and it also makes the three faces of one unit agree with each other, which they did not when the side and top were cut from a sheet they shared with cardboard and perforated steel. The model does NOT honour a stated split: asked for three quarters it drew the vertical seam at 616 and the horizontal one at 512, so MEASURE the seams off the drop (a per-column mean |diff| peaks hard on them) and derive the crops from what it actually drew. lift 0.707 lands the tile at built mean 80.7, the value it shipped at before the swap, so the change is ART and not exposure. AND THE PACK LIFTED THE ASPECT FLOOR: a standalone 1k gen cannot go under about 0.64, because it must clear 655,360 pixels with no edge over 1024, but a SUB-RECT of a sheet has no such floor - this one is 0.6016 and the bookcase got correspondingly narrower, 2.1 -> 1.68 world units.

facility/deco-bookcase-side.prompt: one region of the facility/deco-bookcase-pack.png sheet - the whole prompt is on facility/deco-bookcase-front.
facility/deco-bookcase-side.note: the bookcase's two ends. Its own texture because the first build wore the front's art on them and every bookcase in the compound had book spines running down its sides. corp/facade.note: the nineteen storeys UNDER the floor plate (render.corp.CorpFacade), and the one texture in the corp set that is drawn UNLIT. A MeshBasicMaterial and not a lambert, which is the whole reason the lit bays work: the plate's own lighting has nothing to do with a facade 72 units below it, and under the scene's ambient a lambert would have taken the amber to nothing. Unlit also means the authored value IS the rendered value, so the bays clear BLOOM_THRESHOLD 0.72 on their own and the tower reads as occupied from the parapet. TILED AT 12 WORLD UNITS, which is 2 * FacilityStyle.WALL_H: the image carries exactly two storeys, so one repeat is two 3 m floors and the 6 bays across land at 2 units each. It still takes the scene fog (a basic material is fogged like any other), which is what makes the drop fade out rather than stop. LIFT 2.4, in the DARKENING direction and fitted from the game rather than predicted: the first build put the whole tower at the art's authored value, and unlit that is what renders - a solid wall of gold, every bay reading as lit because the dark glass sat at ~40 srgb where it needed to be black. A gamma is right and a baseColor is not, because what has to move is the RATIO between the bays and the glass and not the level. SAT 0.55 beside it, and the two are answering different things: the gamma sets how MANY bays read as lit (at 2.4 the built sheet was p50 1.1 with 4.6% over 120, which is the right census) and the saturation sets what a hundred of them look like AT ONCE. Authored, the amber is the corp accent hue and correct for one window; tiled over a nineteen-storey tower filling the frame it came out a wall of orange, which is a thing no per-window value can fix.
